about.summary: Buy when the stock starts beating the S&P 500 (its relative-strength line crosses above its 100-day average) while in a long-term uptrend; sell when it starts lagging the market or falls below its 200-day average.
about.why: Momentum is one of the best-documented effects in finance: Jegadeesh & Titman (1993) showed that stocks that outperformed over the past 3-12 months kept outperforming for months afterwards. Gary Antonacci's "dual momentum" combines relative momentum (beating alternatives) with absolute momentum (going up at all), which is what the two conditions here do.
about.caveats: The research ranks many stocks and holds the strongest; one stock's line crossing its average is a looser version. Momentum can reverse violently after market crashes (Daniel & Moskowitz, 2016). Needs S&P 500 data.
references: Jegadeesh, N., & Titman, S. (1993). Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency. The Journal of Finance, 48(1), 65-91.
Antonacci, G. (2014). Dual Momentum Investing. McGraw-Hill.
Daniel, K., & Moskowitz, T. J. (2016). Momentum Crashes. Journal of Financial Economics, 122(2), 221-247.
